newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada dlr ends at 2-year low despite intervention.
newsitem.headline: Canada dlr ends at 2-year low despite intervention.

text.p: FORECAST RANGE 1.3850/1.3895 ASIAN CLOSE 1.3850
RESISTANCE 1.3740 SUPPORT 1.3925 HI 1.3865 LO 1.3840
CANADA OPEN 1.3840/50 HI 1.3925 EUROPE OPEN 1.3843
* Canada's dollar ended weaker at C$1.3925 (US$0.7181) on
Thursday from Wednesday's close of C$1.3850 (US$0.7220)
despite intervention by the Bank of Canada around the C$1.3910
(US$0.7189) level.
* Traders said the currency hit its weakest level since April 4, 1995 under pressure from international investors calling for a rise in interest rates to match one by the Fed.

Traders said one major investor bought US$900 million worth of U.S. treasury bills from the Bank of Canada as others rushed out of Canadian short-term debt to take advantage of the 250 basis point spread between Canadian and U.S. yields.
Analysts pointed out that since the Federal Reserve moved last week the Canadian currency has fallen nearly one U.S. cent from its C$1.3783 (US$0.7255) close on March 25.
Gregory said the currency could test levels as weak as C$1.4200 (US$0.7042) and beyond if the Bank of Canada resists the pressure for higher interest rates and fails to ratify market expections.
"Ratify me baby, ratify me," Gregory said.
Traders and analysts said all eyes will be focused on the U.S. non-farm payrolls report for March, due out on Friday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.

A Reuter survey of economists forecast payrolls to be up 196,000 in March and have said a rise above that could provide further evidence of inflationary pressure in the U.S. economy and increase the likelihood the Fed will raise rates again at the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting in May.
Gregory said the Bank of Canada needs to raise rates to prove that it is no longer prepared to ease monetary conditions.

Economists said the Bank of Canada's resistance to higher rates could place the central bank in the same position it was in at the start of 1995, when its brief resistance a rise in U.S. rates led to a speculative run against Canada's dollar.
Ultimately the Bank of Canada was forced to raise rates sharply in 1995 as a result, arguably placing the economy at risk of recession.
The mid-point of the Bank of Canada's 50 basis point target range for the overnight rate currently is 3.00 percent or 250 basis points below the 5.50 percent Federal funds rate in the U.S.
((Paul Casciato, Reuters Toronto Bureau 416 941-8100 or email: paul.casciato@reuters.com))
